title: Can someone help me understand Wong Kar-wai films?

commenti.body:
You don’t need to like Wong Kar Wai, don’t worry about it haha.

I really like his cinema though, and think he is one of the greatests. I can’t think of an specific book, essay or review to contextualize his films but I’m sure someone else in the replies will help you with that.

Chungkin Express is pure youthful excitement: the music, the over-the-shoulder camerawork, the lights, the dialogue, the way the characters are overdramatic but the film portrais them with tenderness. There is a kinetic energy in this films that really speaks to me and puts me in a good mood.

In the mood for love is equally intense but the intensity is hidden by the characters and the film itself behaves like its protagonists: slow-motion, shots where the camera is behind walls, under stuff, close-ups of hands, objects, surfaces. I’m just getting goosebumps remembering some scenes. I think if you just focus on the story it may seem like nothing special, but if you can understand how the characters are really feeling, and you start engaging with the film like they’re doing with each other, that is, having an eye out for every little detail, every small indication of their true feelings, I think that’s when the movie opens up.
[removed]

I'm the same actually. Watched his films a few years back and found them to be really beautiful but didn't impact me. Hoped rewatching his stuff would make me connect more but it just didn't. Now I haven't seen in the mood for love in a very long time so that could change. 

I think he has a brilliant grasp on the art form, understands why it's special etc, but the meat of his films don't really resonate with me

>I like his style, and I think he is a masterful director and talented, but I just don't like the movies! Why??

Wong Kar-Wai is the epitome of 'style is substance'. All his films revolve around similar themes — romance, heartbreak, loneliness (and urban loneliness), time, memory and nostalgia. Usually his protagonists will have a fatal flaw that keeps them stuck in cycles and unable to grow and/or get together with their true love. 

The urbanised setting of Hong Kong and its relevant sociocultural factors is integral in all his films. In the Mood for Love takes place in the 60's when mass migration from China was happening. His films set in the present day usually feature a lot of Western Capitalist symbols (McDonalds/Cocoa-Cola product placement) to highlight the impact on culture. A lot of the romances can be seen as two lonely people in similar situations trying to make connections.

Most of his films, and especially In the Mood for Love, employ a lot of 'frame-within-a-frame' shots to convey how the characters are 'trapped' by their environment. In ITMFL, it is the sociocultural factors of 1960's Hong Kong that prevent the two from ending up together. Due to the immigration and urbanisation, it is hard to find privacy and intimacy, spaces are very crowded, and two leads are fearful of gossip if they're seen together. 

I remember when first watching Fallen Angels, I was a bit confused throughout the film on the exact 'point' or what he was trying to say with the themes and characters. Then, during the 3rd act, it felt like what I can only describe as the finishing touches to a cinematic painting. 

The hitman repeats the same bit of narration that was in his introductory scene during his death scene, as if to say his lazy tendencies which made him rely on his manager/lover, as well as his immoral occupation as a hitman, were what led to his downfall. But that message was told in such a poetic way, rather than having a bit of exposition through dialogue where the hitman laments on having always lived a lazy and corrupt life. 

Another thing which might help to understand is knowing a bit about his storytelling process. "Most of his films are shot when the script is not yet finished and he builds them in the editing room." Fallen Angels was actually initially meant to be 3rd part to Chungking Express. This is why I like to refer to his films as 'cinematic paintings' — it's as if he's painting a picture about all these aforementioned themes and ideas, rather than telling a specific story with specific, black-and-white meanings and interpretations to take from it.

Happy Together, Chungking Express, In the Mood for Love - all good

The rest of them suck. i found a few of them almost unwatchable.

So, it’s not only u. 

Im 44yo and have been watching his films since the 90’s and my opinions on his films has never changed.
[removed]

It's fine not to like his work. There's plenty of acclaimed directors I dislike. I don't like Oliver Stone, Terrence Malick, Leos Carax etc.

I love Fallen Angels. I especially love the guy breaking into businesses and running them at night - giving people haircuts at night etc. and Chungking Express. But I can't tell you what I like about them. It's mood more than anything. It's just a bunch of people and things happening presented in this odd dreamlike way. It's just nice to get immersed in.

But yes, it doesn't have to be for you. If you don't like it, you don't like it.

Honestly expecting to enjoy In the Mood for Love a lot more on a second viewing: I totally watched it “wrong.” If someone had pitched it to me as >!”two people are clearly in love for years but never sleep together,”!< I would have gotten on its wavelength and felt the tension. But as it is, I spent the whole runtime assuming >!they were sleeping together but the sex scenes were just not being shown to us.!<

Me too. I don't connect with his films at all. I just figured something was lost in the translation that I wasn't getting, but I read over the comments here and think "did we watch the same movie?" because I don't see anything they're seeing.

I feel like there's two kinds of movie lovers. Those who like a great story, and those who like a great experience. Wai is one of those experience filmmakers and I'm much more of a story driven kind of person. I feel the same way about Terrence Malick. I don't think they make bad movies, but when I hear the heaps of praise I just scratch my head and wonder why I can't see it.
[removed]

Art is subjective. Always has been, always will be. It's alright if you just don't "get" the interest around a certain director. That doesn't make you unsophisticated. It just makes you a human being with your own individual tastes and preferences.

There are several revered directors I don't connect with. Won Kar-wai is one of them. It doesn't mean there's anything "wrong" with his films; plainly, there isn't. They speak to millions, they simply don't speak to me.

You aren't his audience, and you don't have to be. Unless someone is challenging you about it (I did once have to defend not loving *In the Mood for Love* at a party) you don't even need to worry about *why*. There are plenty of other films.

Chungking Express is literally lightning in a bottle in the form of a movie. Imagine you’re WKW, first two movies did pretty well and you’re developing a name as an auteur during the golden age of Hong Kong cinema. You start to direct your third feature film *Ashes of Time*, a sprawling marshal arts epic, and halfway through you realize that you don’t have enough money to finish it. So what do you do? 

WKW then scrounges up $100,000, his cinematographer Chris Doyle, and puts together a cast mixed with HK greats such as Tony Leung and Bridgette Lin, and new actors in the names Takeshi Kaneshiro and Faye Wong. With Takeshi Kaneshiro being relatively new to the space, and Faye Wong acting as WKW’s acting discovery. In the years preceding, Faye Wong, after having her first three albums flop as a singer travels to America and “roams around” the streets of New York. She comes back to HK, and she brings with her this incredibly tangible “cool” aura around her, and she subsequently begins to explode in the HK music sphere. This aura that she radiates eventually attracts WKW to cast her in what becomes CK Express.

WKW and Doyle shoot the film in just 23 days, which feels almost instantaneous compared to the sluggish pace at which the production of Ashes of Time was moving. They release the film in HK and it’s a hit. Faye Wong’s career continues to explode as this incredibly cool pop icon, and WKW begins to achieve critical acclaim not just domestically, but overseas, with Tarantino applauding the film and distributing it through his company. 

I think the context in which the film was created is important to my love for the film, because the spontaneity of its production is incredibly tangible as you watch the events on-screen. The movie feels like a raw look into this time capsule of Hong Kong, supposedly at its peak where international influences are abundant but there is this cloud of anxiety that hovers due to the inevitable handover back to the PCR. Chungking Express feels like a movie that could only ever exist in that specific moment of time.
[removed]
[removed]

You should know that WKW was extremely influenced by Godard - he uses what Godard derived from his politics and pursued, both for form and content (for him both went hand in hand), but only in an aesthetic sense, which is the idea of attempting to shoot a moment of truth (a form of presentism if you will).

What is on the screen and what is heard is what matters. WKW's films are all about the present and capturing a specific moment that is all but forgotten and pushed away before you've registered it. For this reason I find his use of slomotion and jagged frames more moving as I age. What may help you is to forget about looking for plot devices, storytelling or structure (though he does indulge in all three) and focus on the image and sound for its own sake. What he achieves is sometimes unreal. Also don't forget to have fun. They're cool, fun, sexy and sooo alive. 

It also helps to have Tony Leung by your side. 

Also regardless of anything, watch Ashes of Time (redux). Maybe the single most important movie of my life.

This is a significantly better explanation and explication than what I've provided for why I don't consume Kar-wai. Until now I've just chalked it up to the "drama" genre, saying his films are a bit too pensieve and slow. 

The way you've explained it, he's almost creating Lynchian explorations of his themes, which is a dynamic way of explaining it (by this I mean he wants the audience to have a sensory experience). That also helps me to further understand why I don't enjoy *some* of his work. Reading the themes, visuals for those themes, and character's operating within those themes is almost akin to book reading for me, which is just too involved for a good portion of my viewing preferences.

Thanks for this!

I think the way he depicts the human desire for love and certain, rather complex feelings that can’t be rationalized (e.g. when in chunking express its said that people want pineapple the one day, but the next day they want something completely else), is just beautiful. if his films don’t do it for you, that’s completely fine. you don’t need a reason for it. I personally couldn’t stand possession the first time I’ve watched it, even though it’s beloved by many and should have been absolutely my kind of film. Rewatched it a while after, and appreciated it a lot more. sometimes it helps revisiting certain pieces of art after a longer period of time. But no one can help you liking his films, haha.
There were sex scenes filmed but WKW left them out the Final Cut , so there is some truth to what you felt .
In the Mood for Love is the greatest depiction of love I've ever seen in film, even more than Lost in Translation which is my favorite movie. Thats all I've seen from War-Kai though.
Highly recommend 2046 then if In The Mood resonated with you.

> 2046 
>An international co-production between Hong Kong, France, Italy, China and Germany, it is a loose sequel to Wong's films Days of Being Wild (1990) and In the Mood for Love (2000). 

interesting, sounds cool I didn't know.
If In The Mood encapsulated love then 2046 manages to encapsulate longing, At least that's how I fell.
This comment should be higher

I saw Lost in Translation in my late 20s, then watched it again last year, some time after I had seen In the Mood for Love for the first time....it's very obvious just how much that film inspired Lost in Translation. I actually caught myself thinking that LiT was a little derivative (still a lovely film).

Turns out, Coppola thanked WKW in her Oscars speech for that movie...not much of a surprise.
